prompt.context: Your client is a record producer looking to bring a new music act to the United States. While traveling through Scandinavia he came across a Swedish Death Metal band he thinks would be a perfect fit for his label. There are currently no Swedish Death Metal bands on US labels and all of their music must be imported from Europe.
prompt.question: Your job is to advise the client whether this is a good idea and give him some launch process suggestions.

clarifying_info.q: What is the difference between an import versus a domestic release?
clarifying_info.a: Imports eat into the margin of the album for the record company and there is no way to price higher.
Yes, this metric includes digital sales.

clarifying_info.q: Is there data on the size of the Swedish Death Metal market in the US?
clarifying_info.a: There are no reliable metrics in the US as this is a relatively new market. The larger Death Metal market will serve as a proxy.

framework: How to introduce the SDM band to the US market: Album Sales, Touring (opening act or headlining act), Late-night television appearances, Music Blogs
Market Size: Total albums sold in US, Size of Death Metal market, Share of the market the SDM band can capture
Customer: Willingness to transition from Death Metal to Swedish Death Metal
Financials: Can the record label charge standard pricing for a new album?

questions.prompt: Last year 150 million albums were sold in the United States. 13% of them were Death Metal. How many Death Metal albums were sold?
questions.guidance: Straightforward percentage calculation. Candidate should multiply 150M by 13% to get 19.5M.

math.setup: Total US albums sold × Death Metal share = Death Metal albums sold

questions.prompt: The Death Metal market is segmented into three groups: hardcore, average, and casual fans. They comprise 20%, 30%, and 50% of the population, respectively. Each group buys 4, 2, and 1.2 albums per person per year. Solve for the size of each group and the amount of albums purchased by each group.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the total fan base of 10 million Death Metal fans (market size proxy). Multiply each segment percentage by 10M to get group size, then multiply by the purchase rate per person.

math.setup: Total Death Metal fans = 10,000,000 (given as market size proxy). Segment size = 10M × segment %. Albums = segment size × albums per person per year.
math.answer: Hardcore: 2M fans, 8M albums; Average: 3M fans, 6M albums; Casual: 5M fans, 6M albums; Total: 20M albums

questions.prompt: We'd like to know the breakeven volume of albums for three marketing programs. Each album is priced at $12. The three marketing options are: Internet - $300k, Internet & Radio - $1mm, and Internet, Radio & TV - $2mm.
questions.guidance: Candidate should divide each marketing cost by the price per album to find the number of albums needed to break even. The key insight is that higher spend options require proportionally more market share to justify.

math.setup: Break-even volume = Marketing cost / Price per album
math.answer: Internet: 25,000 albums; Internet & Radio: ~83,333 albums; Internet, Radio & TV: ~166,667 albums

questions.prompt: Which marketing option would you choose?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask whether the marketing plans target specific fan segments. When told Hardcore = Internet, Average = Radio, Casual = TV, they should recognize that: (1) each plan targets incremental segments; (2) market share required to break even at each tier must be assessed against the relevant segment population; (3) for a genre entirely new to the US, capturing significant market share across average and casual fans is very unlikely. Referencing the 10M total fan base: Internet plan requires ~3.75% market share, Internet & Radio requires ~5%, Internet, Radio & TV also ~5% (based on populations of targeted segments). Candidate should conclude Internet-only is the best option, targeting the most receptive hardcore fans first. Credit should be given if the candidate proactively calculates market share percentages.

math.setup: Market share needed = break-even albums / addressable fan population
steps: Internet targets Hardcore (2M fans): 25,000 / 2,000,000 = 1.25% of hardcore (or ~3.75% noted in casebook relative to 10M total)
Internet & Radio targets Hardcore + Average (5M fans): 83,333 / 5,000,000 = ~1.67% of combined (or ~5% of total per casebook)
Internet, Radio & TV targets all (10M fans): 166,667 / 10,000,000 = ~1.67% of total (or ~5% per casebook)
math.answer: Internet-only plan is correct. Capturing significant share for a sub-genre entirely new to the US is very unlikely, especially when more expensive plans target average and casual fans who are less likely to adopt SDM early. The internet plan requires the lowest absolute volume and targets the most receptive hardcore segment.

brainstorming.prompt: What launch process suggestions would you give the client to successfully introduce the Swedish Death Metal band in the US?

categories.name: Distribution & Sales
ideas: Ensure import logistics are resolved to avoid margin compression

categories.name: Marketing & Promotion
ideas: Internet and music blog campaigns targeting hardcore Death Metal fans
Social media presence in Death Metal communities

categories.name: Touring & Live Performance
ideas: Book band as opening act for established Death Metal acts
Target cities with strong Death Metal fanbases

categories.name: Risk Mitigation
ideas: Pilot with a single before signing a longer-term contract
Build contractual protections around band stability
Consider phased rollout rather than full national launch

recommendation: Client should bring the SDM act to the US using the internet-only marketing plan

This is the first Swedish Death Metal act to be US-based; Death Metal is a niche market and targeting hardcore fans is the best path to gaining initial market share before expanding to broader segments
risks: Band could be a complete flop with no fan adoption
Band could break up before generating returns
Issues such as drug addiction could derail the act
Niche genre may not scale beyond hardcore fans
next_steps: Explore options for pilot launches (e.g., release singles before signing a longer-term contract)
Explore other revenue streams such as touring as an opener for an established act
Pursue appearances on late night television to build mainstream awareness
